```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Li 2026 gave a single oral microdose cocktail of five probe substrates to
Chinese type 2 diabetes patients and pooled their concentrations with the
healthy volunteers (HV) of the same group's earlier cocktail study (Kong
2025). One population PK model was fitted per drug in NONMEM (FOCEI). The
five models were fitted independently, so they are packaged as five model
files that share this article.

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Li_2026_midazolam"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1924307> (open access;
  PMC13561922). The parameter estimates are in Supplementary Table S4.

| Model | Probe for | Structure (Figure 2) | Covariates on the final model |
|-------|-----------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
| `Li_2026_midazolam` | CYP3A | 2-compartment, first-order absorption | gut *Salmonella* abundance on CL/F |
| `Li_2026_dabigatran` | intestinal P-gp (dose given as dabigatran etexilate) | 2-compartment, first-order absorption | serum urea on CL/F; type 2 diabetes on F |
| `Li_2026_pitavastatin` | OATP1B | 2-compartment, parallel first-order and zero-order absorption | sex on CL/F |
| `Li_2026_rosuvastatin` | OATP1B / BCRP | 1-compartment, parallel lagged first-order and zero-order absorption | gut *Clostridium* XIVb abundance and BCRP genotype on CL/F |
| `Li_2026_atorvastatin` | OATP1B / BCRP / P-gp / CYP3A | 2-compartment, zero-order absorption | type 2 diabetes on F |

Parameters are apparent oral values (CL/F, Vc/F, Vp/F, Q/F). Doses are in ug
and concentrations in pg/mL, the paper's units. Elimination is linear in
every model. Inter-individual variability is exponential and residual error
proportional (Methods, 'PopPK modeling').

**Dosing.** Pitavastatin and rosuvastatin split each dose between a depot
(first-order) and a zero-order input straight into `central`: give two dose
records of the full amount, one to `depot` and one to `central` with
`rate = -2`, and the models' `f()` terms apply the split. Atorvastatin is
dosed to `central` with `rate = -2`. Midazolam and dabigatran are dosed to
`depot`.

# Population

Thirteen type 2 diabetes patients (5 male, 8 female; age 49.2 +/- 11.6
years, weight 67.1 +/- 10.0 kg, HbA1c 7.62 +/- 0.77%, disease duration 1.5-8.5
years) and fourteen HV (4 male, 10 female; age 35.6 +/- 13.2 years, weight
58.8 +/- 8.5 kg) completed the study at Peking University Third Hospital (Li
2026 Table 1). All had normal hepatic and renal function (eGFR 103.6 and
106.6 mL/min/1.73 m^2). Seven patients took metformin, two acarbose, two
glyburide and one dapagliflozin. The cocktail (midazolam 10 ug, dabigatran
etexilate 375 ug, pitavastatin 10 ug, rosuvastatin 50 ug, atorvastatin 100
ug) was taken fasted. HV were sampled at 0.5-24 h and patients at 1, 4 and 24
h. Stool microbiome data were available for 9 HV and 8 patients (Figure 3).
The same information is available from
`readModelDb("Li_2026_midazolam")()$population`.

# Virtual cohort

The authors simulated type 2 diabetes patients and HV that differ only in
the covariates linked to diabetes (the diabetes indicator and the gut
*Salmonella* abundance) and share all demographic and genetic
characteristics (Methods, 'PopPK simulation'). This cohort does the same,
with 100 subjects per group:

* *Salmonella* abundance is log-normal with the group mean and SD reported
  in Results ('PopPK analysis'): 0.619 +/- 0.505% (HV) and 0.0880 +/- 0.124%
  (type 2 diabetes).
* Serum urea is normal with the pooled Table 1 mean and SD (4.67 +/- 1.3
  mmol/L), sex follows the pooled 18/27 female fraction, and the BCRP
  rs2231142 GT fraction is the pooled 12/26 of Table S6.
* *Clostridium* XIVb abundance is not tabulated; it is drawn log-normal
  with median 0.0628% (the model's reference value) and a log-SD of 1.2,
  which spans the 0-0.42% range of Figure 3e/f. Its exponent (-0.0847) is
  small, so the choice barely moves rosuvastatin exposure.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20261025)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261025)

n_per_arm <- 100L
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 4, by = 0.1), seq(4.25, 24, by = 0.25))))

drugs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~model, ~dose_ug, ~route,
  "MDZ", "Li_2026_midazolam", 10, "depot",
  "DAB", "Li_2026_dabigatran", 375, "depot",
  "PTV", "Li_2026_pitavastatin", 10, "parallel",
  "RSV", "Li_2026_rosuvastatin", 50, "parallel",
  "ATV", "Li_2026_atorvastatin", 100, "central"
)

rlnorm_meansd <- function(n, m, s) {
  sdlog <- sqrt(log(1 + (s / m)^2))
  rlnorm(n, log(m) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog)
}

shared <- tibble(
  BUN = pmax(rnorm(n_per_arm, 4.67, 1.3), 1.5),
  SEXF = rbinom(n_per_arm, 1, 18 / 27),
  SNP_ABCG2_RS2231142_HET = rbinom(n_per_arm, 1, 12 / 26),
  GUT_CLOSTRIDIUM_XIVB_PCT = rlnorm(n_per_arm, log(0.0628), 1.2)
)
subjects <- bind_rows(
  shared |> mutate(
    group = "HV", DIS_DIAB = 0L,
    GUT_SALMONELLA_PCT = rlnorm_meansd(n_per_arm, 0.619, 0.505)
  ),
  shared |> mutate(
    group = "T2D", DIS_DIAB = 1L,
    GUT_SALMONELLA_PCT = rlnorm_meansd(n_per_arm, 0.0880, 0.124)
  )
) |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)

make_events <- function(subj, dose_ug, route) {
  dose_rows <- switch(route,
    depot = subj |> mutate(cmt = "depot", rate = 0),
    central = subj |> mutate(cmt = "central", rate = -2),
    parallel = bind_rows(
      subj |> mutate(cmt = "depot", rate = 0),
      subj |> mutate(cmt = "central", rate = -2)
    )
  ) |>
    mutate(time = 0, evid = 1L, amt = dose_ug)
  obs <- tidyr::crossing(subj, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, amt = 0, rate = 0, cmt = "central")
  bind_rows(dose_rows, obs) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
sim <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(drugs)), function(i) {
  ev <- make_events(subjects, drugs$dose_ug[i], drugs$route[i])
  rxode2::rxSolve(
    readModelDb(drugs$model[i]),
    events = ev,
    keep = "group"
  ) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    select(id, time, Cc, group) |>
    mutate(drug = drugs$drug[i])
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(
    drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs$drug),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("HV", "T2D"))
  )
```

# Replicate Figure 1 and Figure S3

Li 2026 Figure 1 shows the observed mean (SD) concentrations by group over
0-24 h and Figure S3 overlays the authors' simulated mean and 90% prediction
interval. The simulated mean and 90% prediction interval of this cohort
follow.

```{r figure-1, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
sim |>
  group_by(drug, group, time) |>
  summarise(
    Q05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05),
    mean = mean(Cc),
    Q95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, mean, colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Plasma concentration (pg/mL)",
    colour = NULL, fill = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Replicates Figure 1 / Figure S3 of Li 2026",
      "(mean and 90% PI, 100 subjects per group)."
    )
  )
```

# PKNCA validation

Cmax and AUC0-24 are computed over 0-24 h, the window of Li 2026 Table 2.

```{r pknca}
sim_nca <- sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  mutate(treatment = paste(drug, group)) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, treatment)
sim_nca <- bind_rows(
  sim_nca,
  sim_nca |> distinct(id, treatment) |> mutate(time = 0, Cc = 0)
) |>
  distinct(id, treatment, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(treatment, id, time)

dose_df <- tidyr::crossing(drugs, subjects |> select(id, group)) |>
  mutate(treatment = paste(drug, group), time = 0, amt = dose_ug) |>
  select(id, time, amt, treatment)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, cmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(
  PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals)
)
```

## Comparison against published NCA

The references are the means of the authors' own 1,000-subject simulations
in Li 2026 Table 2 ('HV Sim' and 'Type 2 diabetes Sim'), so the simulated
values below are means too.

```{r nca-compare}
published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment, ~cmax, ~auclast,
  "MDZ HV", 52.2, 136,
  "MDZ T2D", 60.3, 170,
  "DAB HV", 300, 2198,
  "DAB T2D", 369, 2782,
  "PTV HV", 254, 489,
  "PTV T2D", 254, 489,
  "RSV HV", 80.0, 781,
  "RSV T2D", 80.0, 781,
  "ATV HV", 21.1, 143,
  "ATV T2D", 35.7, 245
)

sim_means <- as.data.frame(nca_res) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  group_by(treatment, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(PPORRES = mean(PPORRES), .groups = "drop")

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = sim_means,
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cmax = "pg/mL", auclast = "h*pg/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = "Simulated (mean) vs. Li 2026 Table 2 simulated means. * differs by >20%."
)
```

Every row agrees with the authors' simulations to within 20%. The largest
differences, midazolam Cmax and AUC0-24 (+10% to +17%), follow from the
log-normal *Salmonella* draw: the abundance is skewed, and the authors'
per-subject values are not published.

## Type 2 diabetes versus healthy volunteers, typical values

The paper's headline result is the type 2 diabetes / HV ratio of simulated
exposure (Table 2, last column). With every random effect at zero and the
covariates at their group means, AUC0-24 ratios follow directly from the
diabetes indicator and the *Salmonella* shift.

```{r typical-ratio}
# zeroRe() removes the random effects on purpose; rxode2 warns on every
# multi-subject solve without omega, so muffle that one warning only.
solve_typical <- function(...) {
  withCallingHandlers(
    rxode2::rxSolve(...),
    warning = function(w) {
      if (grepl("without 'omega'", conditionMessage(w), fixed = TRUE)) {
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }
    }
  )
}

typical_subj <- tibble(
  id = 1:2, group = c("HV", "T2D"), DIS_DIAB = c(0L, 1L),
  GUT_SALMONELLA_PCT = c(0.619, 0.0880), BUN = c(4.63, 4.72),
  SEXF = 1L, SNP_ABCG2_RS2231142_HET = 0L, GUT_CLOSTRIDIUM_XIVB_PCT = 0.0628
)
typical <- lapply(c("MDZ", "DAB", "ATV"), function(d) {
  i <- match(d, drugs$drug)
  ev <- make_events(typical_subj, drugs$dose_ug[i], drugs$route[i])
  solve_typical(
    rxode2::zeroRe(rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb(drugs$model[i]))),
    events = ev, keep = "group"
  ) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(auc = sum(diff(time) * (head(Cc, -1) + tail(Cc, -1)) / 2)) |>
    mutate(drug = d)
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = auc) |>
  mutate(
    ratio = T2D / HV,
    published = c(MDZ = 1.25, DAB = 1.27, ATV = 1.71)[drug]
  )
typical |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Drug" = drug, "HV AUC0-24 (h*pg/mL)" = HV,
    "T2D AUC0-24 (h*pg/mL)" = T2D, "T2D/HV (model)" = ratio,
    "T2D/HV (Table 2)" = published
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

# Deterministic: typical values against the authors' simulated ratios. The
# diabetes F factors (1.23, 1.73) and the Salmonella shift fix these to a
# few percent; a mis-transcribed factor moves a ratio by 0.2 or more.
stopifnot(all(abs(typical$ratio - typical$published) < 0.06))
```

The ratios agree to within a few percent. For atorvastatin the ratio is
the relative bioavailability (1.73); for dabigatran it is the bioavailability
(1.23) times the small urea difference; for midazolam it comes entirely from
the lower *Salmonella* abundance of the patients.

# Gut *Salmonella* and midazolam clearance

Eq. 1 makes midazolam CL/F a shallow power function of *Salmonella*
abundance. Over the range of Figure 3a it spans about 0.6- to 1.2-fold of
the reference value.

```{r salmonella, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
tibble(salm = exp(seq(log(0.005), log(1.6), length.out = 100))) |>
  mutate(cl = 57.2 * (salm / 0.187)^0.124) |>
  ggplot(aes(salm, cl)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.0880, 0.619), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Salmonella relative abundance (%)", y = "Typical MDZ CL/F (L/h)",
    caption = "Dashed lines: type 2 diabetes and HV mean abundance (Li 2026 Results)."
  )
```

# Assumptions and deviations

- **Zero microbiome abundance.** Eq. 1 and Eq. 5 are power functions of the
  abundance: an abundance of exactly 0 gives midazolam CL/F = 0 and an
  infinite rosuvastatin CL/F. Figure 3 shows some subjects at or near 0. The
  paper does not state the floor it used, so supply positive values.
- **Missing microbiome data.** Only 17 of 27 participants had stool samples
  (Figure 3). How missing abundances entered the PopPK analysis is not
  stated; the reference values 0.187% and 0.0628% are presumably the
  population medians.
- **BCRP genotype.** 'BCRP DecF' is the rs2231142 GT heterozygote (CPIC);
  no TT homozygote (poor function) was observed, so the model has no factor
  for TT.
- **Dabigatran dose.** The dose is in ug of dabigatran etexilate and the
  concentrations are of dabigatran, so CL/F and the volumes are apparent
  values on the prodrug dose scale.
- **Virtual-cohort covariates.** *Clostridium* XIVb abundance, urea, sex and
  BCRP genotype are drawn from pooled distributions shared by both groups,
  as the authors describe; the per-subject values are not published.
- **Pitavastatin ALAG1** was fixed to 0 (Table S4), so the model has no lag
  on that drug.

# Errata

- **Rosuvastatin F1 exceeds 1 under the stated IIV model.** Table S4 gives
  F1 = 0.668 with omega^2 = 0.615, and the Methods state that all IIV is
  exponential. Taken literally, F1 = 0.668 x exp(eta) exceeds 1 whenever
  eta > log(1 / 0.668) = 0.40, which is about 30% of subjects (SD 0.784),
  and the zero-order fraction 1 - F1 then turns negative, giving negative
  concentrations in the first hours. The paper does not say how this was
  handled. The maintainers cap F1 at 1 (`fdepot <- min(1, exp(lfdepot +
  etalfdepot))`): this keeps the stated exponential form and the omega^2
  scale and changes only the subjects for whom a negative zero-order
  fraction would otherwise arise. In a 1,000-subject HV simulation the capped
  model gives AUC0-24 789 +/- 348 h*pg/mL and Cmax 77.5 +/- 40.9 pg/mL,
  against 781 +/- 326 and 80.0 +/- 35.8 in Table 2. A logit-normal F1 with
  the same omega^2 gives 791 +/- 353 and 78.0 +/- 35.2, indistinguishable
  from the published numbers; the literal uncapped form gives 722 +/- 362,
  with negative concentrations in 318 of 1,000 subjects, and is ruled out.

## Questions for the authors

- How was the exponential IIV on the rosuvastatin first-order fraction F1
  (0.668, omega^2 0.615) kept within [0, 1]? Was F1 truncated at 1, was the
  IIV in fact on a logit scale, or were individual F1 values above 1
  accepted with a negative zero-order fraction?
- How did subjects without stool microbiome data (10 of 27) enter the
  midazolam and rosuvastatin models, and what floor was used for an
  abundance of 0?
